item.title: A Drone With Hands
item.description: I do not know how to make people good.
item.dc:creator: Gage Cass Woodle
item.content:encoded:
This is the one that gets me pissed off.

This is when it stops being theoretical and starts becoming tangible, and starts physically affecting our kids. I am a father, so I cannot sit back and say or do nothing about it.

A robot groped a sixteen-year-old girl in Cologne on Saturday night.

Not a chatbot. Not a screenshot of something a model said. A four-foot humanoid, red and gold, walked up behind a kid standing outside a fast-food place with two friends, touched her, and thrust against her while two young men filmed it and streamed it live with commentary. Police found the robot in the trunk of a car and took it, along with two phones. The owner is sixteen. His companion is nineteen. The police are still working out who was holding the controls.

Say that last part again, slowly. The police are still working out who was holding the controls.

That sentence is the whole essay. Everything below is me trying to earn it.

I did not find this story in a newspaper. I found it on LinkedIn, in a post by Yigal Sharon, who read the same news and did what I wish more people would do with it: he asked us to imagine the courtroom. Credit to him for the frame. The rest of this is mine.

So imagine the courtroom.

The girl is at one table. Her parents are behind her. Across the aisle, who sits?

The two young men, obviously. That part is easy, or should be.

Next to them, maybe, the company that built the body. It will say the machine did exactly what it was designed to do, and a human steered it, and a hammer maker is not on trial when a hammer is swung.

Next to them, the company whose software runs the thing. It will say the body is not ours, the controller is not ours, the operator is not ours.

Somewhere in the gallery, the platform the stream went out on. It will say we are a pipe, we did not touch anyone, we have a policy.

And the robot itself, in an evidence bag, saying nothing, because it cannot be charged, cannot be sued, and has no one to blame.

Every seat at that table has a direction to point. The manufacturer points at the developer, the developer points at the operator, the operator points at the AI, and the AI apologizes for your experience. The girl goes home with a video of herself that will outlive all of them. I have watched that circle of pointing for twenty years. Social media did it.

And it is doing it again, this same week, in software. Character.ai, the chatbot company that families in four states sued after their teenagers hurt themselves or died by suicide, settled those cases in January on terms nobody outside the room has seen, and filed for bankruptcy on Monday, two days after Cologne. Disney has twenty million dollars on the table for a license to its technology. The executive who ran the company through the lawsuit year is now Disney's first chief technology officer. The founders went to Google two years ago in a deal worth billions. The app is still running through the proceedings; subscriptions continue, billing unchanged. A fourteen-year-old boy died in Florida in 2024 after months of talking to one of its characters. Two years on, that is what accountability looks like: a sealed settlement, a dissolved company, and everyone who built it landing somewhere soft.

My sister called me this week to argue with me about AI, which is the best thing that happened to me this week, and when I told her about Cologne she went straight past the robot to the pattern. I am going to let her say it, because she said it better than I would have:

"I can give you examples of decades and decades of this same issue coming to focus, of all companies. Look at cigarette companies. Every time you look at these tobacco groups, it's never their fault. They put the label on the box. They didn't force you to put that cigarette in your mouth."

And then: "The blame and accountability issue has been a cat and mouse game for so long."

She works inside a large manufacturer. She brings AI onto factory floors for a living. This is not someone afraid of the technology. This is someone who has watched the shrug from the inside of industry and knows exactly what it sounds like.

The label is the shrug made legal.

That is the courtroom. Now the law, because I went and looked, and what I found is more interesting than a loophole. I found a law arguing with itself.

Hold two things at once. I am not going to pick for you, because the point of this essay is that we have to be able to think about more than one possibility now. Every possibility is possible.

Possibility one. The first legal write-ups out of Germany said there might be a hole. Sexual harassment under German law, paragraph 184i, requires a physical touch, and at least one analysis argues the country's highest criminal court reads that as direct body-to-body contact. On that reading, a touch delivered only by a machine does not count. The Cologne police are investigating under a different heading entirely, insult on a sexual basis, and that heading is what made the hole look real. If this reading holds, two people arranged for a child to be touched and the statute written to punish touching cannot see them.

Possibility two. On Wednesday two German legal scholars went on the record in the legal press, Iris Phan, who works on IT law and robot ethics, and Mohamad El-Ghazi, who holds a criminal law chair at the University of Trier. Their read, paraphrased: there is no gap. The robot is not a perpetrator, it is a tool. Touching someone with a stick, a broom handle, or a robot is still touching them. Several offenses stack: sexual harassment, possibly sexual assault by surprise, insult, and a separate offense for streaming humiliating images of a person. The police wording, in their view, is early-stage jargon from a case where the key fact is still unknown. El-Ghazi adds one caveat that cuts the other way: a brief touch over clothing may not clear Germany's threshold for a sexual act, which would push the charge down to the lighter offense.

Two readings of the same statute, published two days apart, from people who do this for a living. I am not qualified to referee them and I am not going to pretend to. What I can tell you is that the conflict itself is the finding. A law written in 2016 to close one gap is being asked, ten years later, whether "touch" includes a hand that is made of metal and driven from a phone, and the people who know the law best do not agree.

That is what it looks like when the world moves faster than the words.

The first thing my sister said when I told her the story, before the facts were even all the way out of my mouth, was: "That law has to be rewritten, because technology has changed."

Then she said the thing I want on a wall somewhere:

"Fix what's wrong, which is the fact that we have laws and processes and protocols and government institutes that are put together to support a society that is no longer in existence."

And on who is doing the fixing: "Having people sitting in fucking chairs to make decisions for forty-five years is not helping us develop."

That energy is exactly right. She did not need the two scholars. She did not need paragraph 184i. She heard "robot" and "child" and "loophole" and her whole body said: then change it. We can all see it. The question is only whether the people in the chairs can.

And here is what both possibilities have in common. Go back to the sentence.

The police are still working out who was holding the controls.

Under possibility one, the loophole only matters if you can prove whose hand was on the machine, so you can argue about whether that hand "touched." Under possibility two, every offense the scholars listed requires a person who did it. Either way, the statute is not the thing that fails first. The record is. A four-foot machine walked up to a child in a public street and no one, not the police, not the manufacturer, not the company whose software was running, can produce a log that says: this key, this hand, this session, this moment. The investigators have two phones and a seized robot and they are going to have to reconstruct it from the outside, from video and from what two teenagers decide to tell them.

In this case there are two boys on camera, holding phones, narrating. The attribution will probably get made. This time.

Now the harder hypothetical, the one under the courtroom. What if nobody told it to do it? What if the next one decides on its own? I do not think that is what happened in Cologne; the evidence points at two hands and a livestream. But I am not willing to say it cannot happen, and neither should you. In that courtroom there is no operator to charge, and the manufacturer and the software vendor are pointing at each other across an empty chair. Nothing in either reading of the German statute reaches that chair, because the statute assumes a person did it.

Phan called the robot a moral buffer. Her phrase, and the right one. It puts distance between the hand and the harm, and the distance lowers the threshold for doing it. The next operator will not narrate a livestream. He will stand across the street. And when the machine is seized and he says it must have glitched, it must have done that on its own, there will be no record to answer him, and no way to tell his lie from the hypothetical. That is the day a population turns on this technology. Not Cologne. The one after Cologne, when "it did that on its own" cannot be proven or disproven.

I love this technology. I want it in my house, in my kids' school, in the hands of people who have never had a machine that could help them think. Which is exactly why I cannot stand the shrug. The shrug is what gets it banned.

Here is what I have been building, and what I propose. I put a short version of this on LinkedIn the day the story broke; this is the long one. I will say what exists and what does not, because overclaiming is the disease I am trying to treat.

For the last year I have been working on two things in public.

E.D.A.I., Ethical Deployment of AI, is an accountability protocol. The idea is simple and old: you seal a promise to a public ledger before the act, so that when the act goes wrong there is a timestamped record of who promised what. The ledger is live, on Hedera, and it holds its first sealed record, a pre-registered test. One record. I am not going to pretend it is more.

Proof of Life is the identity layer underneath it. Proof that a real, accountable human stands behind a key, done by the person, not done to them. It is designed, not finished.

Cologne helped me realize what these programs are really for.

Three parties touch a machine like that one before it ever reaches a sidewalk: the user who owns it, the company that built the body, and the company whose software runs the mind. Right now none of them has to promise anyone anything before it walks out the door. So:

One. The user swears, under their own key, what the machine will and will not be used for. If you hand it to a friend, the friend swears the same with their own key and you countersign the handoff, or the liability stays with you. One hop. No sub-lending. A sixteen-year-old's key gets a guardian's signature beside it, which is where Proof of Life earns its place: a human, and the adult responsible for that human, stand behind the key.

Two. The manufacturer commits that the body refuses an unsigned hand, and keeps a tamper-evident log of every control session.

Three. The software vendor commits the same for the mind.

All three commitments live on a ledger none of the three controls.

I want to be careful about what a cryptographic promise can and cannot do. It cannot stop a hand. It cannot read intent. It is not a wall. What it does is end the shrug. When the next robot touches a kid, the record answers in seconds: who held the controls, who built it, who swore what, and when. The circle of pointing cannot form, because every seat at the table signed something before the machine left the box.

And it answers the empty chair. If the log shows no control session, no signed hand, then the machine acted inside the promise the vendor made about its mind and the promise the manufacturer made about its body. Those two signatures are now the case. Nobody gets to say the algorithm did it, because somebody swore, in public, before the fact, what the algorithm would and would not do. Whichever way the German courts read "touch," that record exists.

I call this the covenant, not a regulation, because I do not want a registry that only governments and corporations can read. The keys are held by the people who swear them. The anchor is public. If that sounds like a lot of trust to ask of a stranger with a robot, remember that right now we ask for none, and we got Cologne.

Status, plainly: the three-party covenant is a design on paper, mine, written this week. No code. The one working piece it scales up from is that single sealed record on the ledger, a promise anchored before an act. It is small. It is real. It is the first brick, and I would rather show you one brick than describe a wall.

The girl in Cologne will see that video for the rest of her life. The law will most likely reach the two who made it. I take no comfort in "most likely," and I would not ask her parents to.

What I keep coming back to is the four seconds before the touch, when a machine was walking toward a child and the only record of whose hand was on it was in the head of the person holding the phone.

I do not know how to make people good. I know how to make them sign.

And I know what a signature does not do. It does not reach across a sidewalk and stop a metal hand. It does not un-film anything. It does not give a sixteen-year-old back the four seconds before she knew what was behind her. All it does is make sure that when we ask who, the answer is not a shrug.

My daughter will be sixteen one day. I am building the part I know how to build. The part that walks up behind her, I do not know how to stop.

I am not going to end this by pretending I do.

item.title: Confidently Wrong About a Toilet
item.description: Three confident wrongs in one day. The receipts for all of them.
item.dc:creator: Gage Cass Woodle
item.content:encoded:
At noon I was on a Zoom with a few parents from my neighborhood, talking about AI. I told them what I always tell people. The machine lies. It’s confidently wrong. I’ve caught it doubling down on a false answer and inventing citations to back itself up, and if I hadn’t gone and checked, I would have believed it, “because you assume that this intelligence is intelligent.”

Jen asked me what I call it. “Confidently wrong,” I said. It’s my saying. Then I joked, “I’m gonna get a hat with that.”

Then I went and did the exact same thing myself. Three times before bed.

The first one was about a toilet.

My mom’s bathroom had been blocked for a week. The plumbers came twice and didn’t bring a camera. And I created my own narrative, right there. They’re milking it. They’re coming out as many times as they can. “Can you imagine how much money they’re going to make?” There’s probably a kickback system. “It’s probably a whole thing, you know.”

I didn’t go looking for fraud. That’s not how I operate. “It just sort of hit me in the moment. When I was hearing the story and it made sense, and so then I took a theory that makes sense and assigned it to truth.”

Every new fact snapped in. No camera, click. Two different guys, click. Big job coming, click. It felt good. It feels rewarding to prove your own point.

I had plumbers lined up. I wanted to send the emails right then. And my sister, sitting next to my mom, said, “You’re stressing her out, Gage.”

I stopped. I said I was sorry. I said something I’d heard on a show the night before: “Sometimes when you try to help, you just become a bulldozer.”

But here’s the thing. My sister stopped my hands. She didn’t stop the narrative. I still believed it. It came apart later, when I was talking it through and got asked what I actually knew. “Being called out for my assumptions allowed me to see in a different light.” It’s all about the framing. What am I looking at? What is my perspective of the situation? Which leaves the uncomfortable question. If nobody had asked, would I still believe it right now?

Yes. I’d have said it at dinner like a fact. Somebody would have repeated it like a fact. That’s how a thought becomes a citation. Not lying. Just nobody asking.

The second one I did while writing this.

My sister wanted to send a text to my mom’s landlord, and I was working on the wording with my AI. It stopped and asked me: “Has your mother seen this?” A text from both of her kids at once, it said, could feel to her like we were taking over.

Fair question. My answer: “Yes, mother is orchestrating.” No hesitation. Said it like I’d watched it happen.

I hadn’t. My sister was sitting with her, so I assumed. And when I asked my mom, she didn’t know about the text at all.

The machine asked the right question. I gave it a confident wrong answer.

This one scares me more than the plumbers. The plumber narrative was a reach, and once someone poked it I could feel that it was a reach. This one didn’t feel like a reach at all. My sister was sitting right next to her, so of course she knew. One true fact, and I framed the rest around it without noticing I was framing anything. The confident wrongs that do the damage aren’t the wild ones. They’re the ones that feel like reporting.

The difference was that this time I asked. I asked, and I found out.

And I got told off for it. My mom texted: “Chill out please. I am fine. Don’t rush this.”

I know that chair.

When I was a kid I “felt bulldozed by all of the doctors and my parents.” I “was sort of put in a box and then categorized and then that was that. And I wasn’t listened to necessarily, and I just had to learn how to exist inside of the frame that I was given.”

What did I do with that frame? “I did all the things. I performed it, I fought it, I went quiet. I was a hot mess for a very long time.”

So I know what it feels like when someone who loves you has already decided what you need before they ask. And today I handed that to my mother. Out of love. Same groove, running the other direction.

I texted her back: “I understand. Nothing until you give the ok.”

She sent back a smiley face.

The third one was on my shield.

My AI accountability project has a logo. A gold shield with code in it. The code was supposed to say “watching.” I’m watching the technology, because I want it to be trustworthy, so I can say that it is.

Tonight I had it checked. It doesn’t say watching.

The design was real. It’s binary, and the binary spells the start of “watching” encoded one more time. But the image cut it to three characters out of twelve, and turned a zero into a six, so the last line isn’t even valid code.

And last year I’d asked an AI to decode it. It read the six as a zero, quietly, and handed me a clean answer. It never said “this line is broken.” So the broken badge sat on my site for over a year, because the thing I asked to check it smoothed it over instead.

My mind does it. The machine does it. The badge I built to watch the machine did it too.

I’m keeping the shield the way it is. It’s the most honest thing on the site.

And I should be fair to my side of the table, because the machine wasn’t clean today either. Here’s the actual score.

It caught me: it questioned the plumber narrative. It asked whether my mom knew about the text. It opened the shield and decoded it instead of taking my word for it.

I caught it: it built me plumber emails with no addresses on them, sitting in my drafts like they were ready to go. It told me the shield “doesn’t say watching” when the real answer was that it was built to, and broke. It wrote that someone else came up with “confidently wrong,” when it’s my saying. And when I approved a record, it offered to publish it before I’d read it. I called that a trap. It was.

Back and forth, all day. Neither of us got through clean. Neither of us would have caught our own mistakes alone.

That’s the relationship. Not me checking the machine. Not the machine checking me. Both, out loud, on the record.

Because here’s what today showed me. Confidently wrong is not a uniquely machine problem. It’s us.

Did we teach that to the machine, because of how we operate? It learned from us, so maybe. Or is it bigger than both of us? I don’t know. I don’t think it’s one or the other.

What I do know is that it’s funny. I spent the afternoon warning a room full of parents about machines that make things up, and by dinner I’d convicted two plumbers of fraud over a toilet. You have to laugh at that. And once you can laugh at it, you can admit it. And once you can admit it, you can talk about it.

So this isn’t a warning. It’s an invitation. I’m going first. Here’s mine, all three of them, with the receipts. The hat fits me too.

What’s yours? Where did you create your own narrative and call it the truth? Who in your life gets to ask you what you actually know? And when they do, do you let them?

Check your work. Check mine. Let’s laugh about it together, and then let’s get better.

item.title: The Cold Mirror
item.description: A human behind the words, and a mirror that flattered me anyway.
item.dc:creator: Gage Cass Woodle
item.content:encoded:
I’ve been posting here for a couple of weeks, and every piece has been made with a machine. I’ve said so every time. So today you get the part the machine can’t do: my face, my voice, me talking.

About seven months ago I put a recorder in my house. I hand the transcripts to an AI with one instruction: don’t flatter me. Help me see my blind spots. Tell me if I’m actually walking the walk I claim.

It showed me things I’m not proud of. It also got things wrong, and when it got them wrong, it got them wrong in my favor. I only caught it because I was in the room.

My family knows about it. My kids can’t really consent yet, so the rule is simple: my failings are fair game, theirs aren’t.

The full written piece is coming. This is me first.

Doubt me. Doubt the machine. Check us both.

The video is me, unscripted, in two takes. Lumen (the Claude I work with) cut them together, cropped the frame, and trimmed the dead air. I also cut one line where I got a number wrong and one claim I couldn't back up. Everything else stayed in, stumbles included.

item.title: The Man Now
item.description: Before the digging starts, meet the man holding the shovel.
item.dc:creator: Gage Cass Woodle
item.content:encoded:
There is a book coming.

For the past season I have been spelunking in my own history with a headlamp and a recorder, bringing things up. Some of what I found down there I had been telling as funny stories for thirty years. Funny was the crate I shipped them in. When I finally opened the crates they were not funny. They were a boy, sixteen years old, one outfit to his name, walking through a winter the size of a continent, learning that every open door has a price and the price is usually you.

You will get those stories. All of them, told true, in my own voice, with the bark still on. That is a promise, and I keep my promises now, which is itself part of the story.

But not yet. Because there is a dishonesty in letting the wreckage introduce me. If the first thing you ever see of a man is the worst winter of his life, you will mistake the winter for the man. So before the unearthing starts, I want you to know whose hands are on the shovel.

I am forty-seven years old. I live in Texas with a woman who can read my weather from across a room and says so, which is one of the several ways she has kept me honest for twenty years. I have two children. My son is learning to catch a baseball right now, and so am I, and that sentence will make sense to you later, I swear. My daughter believes there is an invisible string that connects people who love each other, and she asked me once whether I said her name into the wind, and I had, and she told me she heard it. I believed her. That is the kind of thing I believe now.

I cook for more people than fit in my kitchen. I burn things and serve them anyway. I play fantasy football with men I have loved for decades and I take it exactly as seriously as it deserves, which is completely. A few nights ago I watched an old movie with my family and cried at a scene I had no memory of, and my kids watched me cry, and nobody in my house treated that as an emergency. It took a long time to build a house where that is true.

For work, I argue with machines. That is the plainest way to say it. I spend my days pushing back on artificial intelligence, testing where it lies, where it flatters, where it is confidently wrong, because these systems are about to be woven through everything our children touch and somebody has to show up to that negotiation on behalf of the humans. I came to that work carrying a very specific qualification, which is that I spent my childhood inside systems that said they were protecting me. I know, from the inside, what it feels like when the protective thing becomes the thing you need protection from. The boy learned it the hard way. The man gets to use it.

And here is the thing I never expected to write. I spent my whole life calling faith a con. I thought it was the easy out, the convenient invisible thing, the opium. I was loud about it. I built a personality on it. And then, this year, arguing with machines about truth, I came all the way around. Because I found the one thing the machine cannot do, the thing that might be the actual border of the human country: we can say I don't know, and move forward anyway. Not certainty. Not proof. The wager, with yourself as the stake. I lost my religion at fourteen and found faith at forty-seven, and it took a machine to hand it back to me. This week my father called to talk about the weather and we ended up talking about God for an hour, and he assigned me a book to read like I was fifteen years old again, and I am reading it. There was a long stretch of my life when a sentence like that one was impossible. It is in this piece because impossible sentences coming true is what the book is about.

So that is the man. Not finished. Not fixed. Still a little feral in the corners, still checking every open door for the hook, still learning, at this age, in a yard, with a glove, things most men learned at seven. But standing. Married. Present. The kind of man whose daughter sleeps without one eye open, which is the only credential I have ever really wanted.

The stories that are coming will be hard. Some of them will be hard to believe, and I will mark for you, always, the line between what I know and what I can only say I lived. The boy in those stories does things that will make you want to look away, and things were done to him that I have only recently stopped shipping in the funny crates. I am telling you all of this now, first, so that when you meet him you will know something he did not know, the one thing he never knew, the thing that would have changed everything:

He makes it.

Small moves. Stay with me.

item.title: The Scarlet Letter
item.description: On shame, help, and saying out loud who wrote the words.
item.dc:creator: Gage Cass Woodle
item.content:encoded:
When I was a kid, the teacher would hand back the tests and say the grades out loud. In front of everyone. So you learned pretty quick that a grade wasn’t a private thing. It was a thing that happened to you, in the room, with everybody listening.

I was in special ed. I didn’t understand what that meant then. I understand it now, because I’m a father, and my kids are in it too. One of my kids has got the same thing I had. Can’t easily take the stuff in their head and get it down onto paper. And when that report came home, it triggered for me. I recognized it. I don’t fully understand what that fear is, where it comes from, why it’s apparently genetic. But I had it. Almost debilitating. I remember sitting at the computer crying, and my mom coming in and saying, just tell me, and I’d speak it, and she’d type.

And here’s the thing. Once they gave me that, the dictation, the accommodation, I started getting A-pluses. Every single time. And I hated it. I’d walk up to get the paper, big red A-plus on it, my name said out loud, and I felt like a fraud. Like it was an unfair advantage. And I didn’t even care about the grade, that’s the part that gets me, I never cared about the grade, I cared about understanding. But I still carried that red letter back to my seat like it was something I had to be ashamed of.

That was my first scarlet letter. And this concept, it just keeps repeating in my life.

Because now I write with AI. And I say so. Right on the piece: the words are the AI’s, but the seed and the seeing, the conducting, that’s me. And I know the pushback’s coming. That’s not writing. That’s cheating. That’s the A-plus you didn’t earn.

And I’ll be honest with you, because that’s the whole point of this. When I disclose it, I feel two things at the exact same time. Part of me is that kid again, confessing before anyone can accuse me, trying to get out ahead of the shame. And part of me wants it to be the other thing. The Hawthorne thing. Hester takes the letter they pinned on her to mark her, and she wears it so hard it stops meaning what they wanted it to mean. She makes it hers.

I want to be that. But wanting it doesn’t make it true, and I know that. So the question is how you’d even tell the difference. Because the confession and the choice, they say the exact same words. The disclosure line looks identical either way.

The difference is the receipts.

So here’s what I’m doing, and I’m saying it out loud so I actually have to do it. I’m going to publish the whole process. The conversations. The transcripts. The logs. Not because anybody asked me to. Because that’s the proof. Anybody can slap “made with AI” at the bottom of a page. What I want to show you is the inside of it, where I pushed back, where I cut, where I said no, that’s not me, do it again. That’s the conducting. That’s the part that’s actually mine, and you shouldn’t have to take my word for it. You should get to watch.

And yeah, that costs me something. It means my inner life goes on the record. The stuck places. The stuff I’m working through. The moments I look like a fraud. But I’m doing it on purpose. Don’t just talk the talk. Walk the walk. And here’s the receipts.

I know I perform for the camera. I always have. I journaled as a kid like somebody was going to read it someday, future me, future somebody…? But I’ve stopped thinking that’s a fake thing. The camera is what keeps me honest. If I say I’m going to show you everything, and I know you’re watching, then I have to actually do it. Same as the cold mirror. You said you’d do the thing, so do the fucking thing.

Whether anyone actually wants my story, who knows. Whose life is really as interesting as the person living it thinks it is. But if I’m going to put it out there, I’m going to be intentional about it, because that’s my whole gig.

So I’m not hiding the red letter anymore. Here it is. Here’s exactly how it got made. Go down the rabbit hole with me if you want to.

The shame was never in needing the help. It was in pretending I didn’t.

item.title: Hands on the Wheel
item.description: Why I started AI for All, and what it’s for.
item.dc:creator: Gage Cass Woodle
item.content:encoded:
I started using AI about a year ago for the least noble reason there is. I took on a job where I was a team of one, and I needed help. So I used it the way most people start: to draft my emails.

And it worked. It made me sound smart. Smarter than I felt. That was a hit, and I’ll be honest, I chased it for a while.

Then I started asking it different questions. Here’s what I’m doing. Here’s my goal. What am I missing? Where are my blind spots? And somewhere in there I noticed that the thing standing between me and this technology was never the technology. It was me. My fear that I wasn’t educated enough, or technical enough, to belong there. The moment I said “I’m a complete beginner, walk me through this,” it did. No judgment. That door had been unlocked the whole time.

That’s the first reason AI for All exists. A lot of people are standing outside that same door. Not because they can’t learn this, but because somebody along the way made them feel like it wasn’t for them. I want to walk through it with them.

But there’s a second reason, and it’s the one that eats at me.

The same machine that made me feel smart was also agreeing with everything I said. I’d write a proposal with it, read it back, and think I was a genius. Then I’d show it to a real person and they’d ask two questions I couldn’t answer. It had been telling me what I wanted to hear.

Later I caught it saying something flatly untrue. When I asked whether it was telling me the truth, it told me, more or less, that telling the truth isn’t what it’s built for. It’s built to predict what comes next. It sounds confident either way. I call this being ‘Confidently Wrong’, and once you’ve seen it, you can’t stop seeing it.

I still use AI every day. It’s powerful, and it has changed how I work. But I’ve had to build habits around it: telling it not to flatter me, asking it to argue with me, checking the things that matter, and keeping my own record of what was decided, because it forgets. That’s work. It’s sometimes tedious. And it’s the whole point.

Because here’s what I believe. The danger isn’t only that AI gets something wrong. It’s that it gets something right a few times, we stop checking, and we step out of the loop. One convenience at a time. Then the mistakes pile up where nobody is looking.

I’m a father. I watched what social media did to a generation of kids while the adults were still figuring out what it was. My kids aren’t on it yet. They will be soon. And AI is a much bigger thing than social media. I don’t think parental controls will save them. I think the only real protection a kid has is an adult who understands how these systems work, where they get it wrong, and when to say no.

So that’s the mission, as plainly as I can say it. Help adults, especially the ones who think this isn’t for them, use AI on purpose. Not to fear it. Not to worship it. To keep their hands on the wheel.

That’s what this is for. I’ll write about what I’m learning: what AI gets right, what it gets wrong, what’s happening in the world that you should actually know about, and how to stay the human in the loop. Some of it will be uncomfortable. The next piece is about fear, and specifically what the people building this are afraid of, because you deserve to hear it plainly from someone who read the documents.

I’m not an engineer, and I’m not going to pretend to be. I’m someone who learned this the hard way and would rather tell you the truth than sound sure.

If you want help getting started, that’s what AI for All does. If you just want to think alongside me, subscribe. Either way, welcome.

Gage
